title: Calum Ciar stands where an heir stands
summary: In the first sharing of his mother's own holding, Calum Ciar stands a pace behind Eilidh Ghlas's shoulder at the bank, and the ford takes notice of him for the first time. No one at Dùn ìseal afterward looks for another heir.

title: Eilidh weighs the old custom of the valleys
summary: Eilidh Ghlas turns over, without acting on it, a custom she learned as a girl in the near valleys: that a household with two sons sometimes sends the younger to be raised at another hearth, so that he grows up loved rather than waiting on an inheritance not his.

title: The younger son born in a high river spring
summary: A second son is born to Eilidh Ghlas at Dùn ìseal in a wet spring, when the river at Àth shean runs high enough to float the ford-stones. No reciter keeps his day, and none ever will.

title: A boy who does not ask to ride out
summary: Eilidh's younger son, six years old, watches his brother ride out with the men to renew the boundary stones and does not ask to go. His mother watches him a long while from the hall door and tells her steward that a house with only one door out of it is no house for a second son.

title: Word sent west to the Red Hill
summary: Eilidh Ghlas sends word to Lachlann Ruadh, holder of the Red Hill, asking that he take her younger son to be raised in his household. She gives it out as a mother's wish that the boy learn a trade of his own; the ford's peace is served by it besides.

title: Calum Ciar counts the miles at the gate
summary: On the morning his brother leaves for the Red Hill, Calum Ciar stands long at the gate after the party is out of sight, and tells a groom who asks him in out of the wind that he is only counting how many days fifty miles there and back will take.

title: Eilidh's parting at Àth shean
summary: Eilidh Ghlas walks with her son's party as far as Àth shean and kneels to his height at the turning of the roads, telling him he is not sent for any wrong of his, that the Red Hill will be as much home to him as Dùn ìseal, and that she means to see him grown.

title: A mound left untouched on the salt road
summary: On the road west, the household man Donnchadh stops before a low green mound and will go no nearer to it, telling the boy only that it is older than the road and the salt trade. A wise traveller, he is told, lets such places lie as he lets a wasp's nest lie.

title: Rìonach's saying of the forked river
summary: Turning off the salt road for her own kin at Àth shean, Rìonach tells the fosterling that a household not his own by birth is no loss to him but a doubling, as a forked river becomes two whole rivers rather than two lesser ones.

title: The fosterling comes to the Red Hill
summary: Eilidh Ghlas's younger son comes down to the western lake shore at evening and is met at the gate by Lachlann Ruadh and his daughter Peigi, who tells her father plainly that he is too thin and will need feeding, and carries in his one bundle herself.

title: Lachlann forbids the naming of a king's son
summary: Lachlann Ruadh tells his household that the fosterling is to be called no king's son and no king's grandson, but a boy of the ford's people come to learn a trade, and warns his daughter Peigi he will hear of it if she names him otherwise again.

title: Calum Ciar given the boundary stones
summary: Calum Ciar is given the judging of the near valleys' boundary stones, the first trust of its kind laid on him, and settles a dispute between two herders over a shifted marker with a plainness his mother is said to have approved of.

title: The fosterling first put out on the lake
summary: The fosterling is let out on Loch chrom in a boat for the first time, and comes back to the Red Hill wet through and pleased with himself, word of it carried east along the salt road to Dùn ìseal by the carriers who walk it.

title: Eilidh Ghlas visits the Red Hill
summary: Eilidh Ghlas comes to the Red Hill as Lachlann Ruadh's guest and sits at his own board four days, asking after the tallies and the weather as she asks after her son. Walking with her son to the western point of the lake, she tells him she will not come again for some years.

title: The fosterling rakes salt without breaking the crust
summary: Lachlann Ruadh puts a salt-rake into the fosterling's hands on the drying platform above Loch chrom and shows him the turn of the wrist his own family has kept for generations. By the fourth stroke the boy lifts a clean sheet of crust whole, and Peigi Dhubh tells him it is better than she managed her own first year.

title: The Red Hill list begins to call Lachlann of the fostering
summary: In these years the Red Hill's reciters take up the habit of naming Lachlann Ruadh also Lachlann an Altraim, Lachlann of the fostering, until in time the second name is given by the list where the first once stood, and is never afterward unsaid.
